claim: NPC1 is a polytopic membrane protein with 13 transmembrane helices.
source: Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) is a polytopic membrane protein with 13 transmembrane helices that exports LDL-derived cholesterol from lysosomes by carrying it through the 80 Å glycocalyx and the 40 Å lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of NPC1's structure.

claim: NPC1 exports LDL-derived cholesterol from lysosomes by carrying it through the 80 Å glycocalyx and the 40 Å lipid bilayer.
source: Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) is a polytopic membrane protein with 13 transmembrane helices that exports LDL-derived cholesterol from lysosomes by carrying it through the 80 Å glycocalyx and the 40 Å lipid bilayer.
evidence: This describes the functional role of NPC1 in cholesterol transport, including specific structural dimensions.

claim: Cholesterol transport begins when cholesterol binds to the N-terminal domain (NTD) of NPC1.
source: Transport begins when cholesterol binds to the N-terminal domain (NTD) of NPC1, which projects to the surface of the glycocalyx.
evidence: This describes the initial step in the cholesterol transport mechanism.

claim: The NTD of NPC1 projects to the surface of the glycocalyx.
source: Transport begins when cholesterol binds to the N-terminal domain (NTD) of NPC1, which projects to the surface of the glycocalyx.
evidence: This describes the spatial positioning of the NTD relative to the glycocalyx.

claim: When co-expressed, the NTD fragment and the remaining portion of NPC1 reconstitute cholesterol transport.
source: When co-expressed, the two NPC1 fragments reconstitute cholesterol transport, indicating that the NTD has the flexibility to interact with the remaining parts of NPC1 even when not covalently linked.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: The NTD has the flexibility to interact with the remaining parts of NPC1 even when not covalently linked.
source: When co-expressed, the two NPC1 fragments reconstitute cholesterol transport, indicating that the NTD has the flexibility to interact with the remaining parts of NPC1 even when not covalently linked.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results showing functional complementation.

claim: Cholesterol can be transferred from the NTD of one full-length NPC1 to another NPC1 molecule that lacks the NTD.
source: We also show that cholesterol can be transferred from the NTD of one full-length NPC1 to another NPC1 molecule that lacks the NTD.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding of the study.

claim: Cholesterol is transported through interactions between two or more NPC1 molecules.
source: These data support the hypothesis that cholesterol is transported through interactions between two or more NPC1 molecules.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Cholesterol enters mammalian cells through the receptor-mediated uptake of plasma low density lipoprotein (LDL).
source: Cholesterol enters mammalian cells through the receptor-mediated uptake of plasma low density lipoprotein (LDL) (Brown and Goldstein, 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous work.

claim: After its liberation from LDL in lysosomes, cholesterol is bound by NPC2.
source: After its liberation from LDL in lysosomes, cholesterol is bound by a soluble intralysosomal carrier protein designated Niemann-Pick C2 (NPC2), which delivers it to a membrane-embedded transport protein designated NPC1 (Pentchev, 2004).
evidence: This describes the role of NPC2 in cholesterol transport, supported by citation.

claim: NPC2 delivers cholesterol to NPC1.
source: After its liberation from LDL in lysosomes, cholesterol is bound by a soluble intralysosomal carrier protein designated Niemann-Pick C2 (NPC2), which delivers it to a membrane-embedded transport protein designated NPC1 (Pentchev, 2004).
evidence: This describes the functional interaction between NPC2 and NPC1.

claim: Niemann-Pick C disease is a fatal lysosomal lipid storage disease caused by mutations in NPC1.
source: Successful elucidation of this transport mechanism will provide a paradigm for the transport of a lipid across a membrane, and it will also advance the understanding of Niemann-Pick C disease, a fatal lysosomal lipid storage disease caused by mutations in NPC1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the disease etiology.

claim: NPC1 is a complex protein of 1278 amino acids with 13 transmembrane helices and three structured lumenal domains.
source: NPC1 is a complex protein of 1278 amino acids with 13 transmembrane helices and three structured lumenal domains (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the structural composition of NPC1, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Cholesterol-loaded NPC2 binds to the middle lumenal domain (MLD) of NPC1.
source: Cholesterol-loaded NPC2 binds to one of these domains designated the middle lumenal domain (MLD), which positions NPC2 so that it can transfer its cholesterol to the N-terminal domain (NTD) (Deffieu and Pfeffer, 2011).
evidence: This describes the binding interaction between NPC2 and NPC1, supported by citation.

claim: The MLD positions NPC2 so that it can transfer its cholesterol to the NTD.
source: Cholesterol-loaded NPC2 binds to one of these domains designated the middle lumenal domain (MLD), which positions NPC2 so that it can transfer its cholesterol to the N-terminal domain (NTD) (Deffieu and Pfeffer, 2011).
evidence: This describes the functional consequence of NPC2-MLD binding.

claim: The NTD must transfer its cholesterol across the ~80 Å glycocalyx to reach the membrane domain of NPC1.
source: The NTD then must transfer its cholesterol across the ~80 Å glycocalyx so that it can reach the membrane domain of NPC1 (Neiss, 1984).
evidence: This describes a key step in the cholesterol transport mechanism with a specific distance measurement.

claim: The transfer of cholesterol from the NTD to the membrane is believed to require the interaction of the NTD with the Ω loop in the C-terminal domain (CTD).
source: This transfer is believed to require the interaction of the NTD with a 9-amino acid loop designated the Ω loop in the C-terminal domain (CTD) (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a proposed mechanism for cholesterol transfer, supported by citation.

claim: The membrane domain of NPC1 contains a sterol-sensing domain (SSD) composed of five transmembrane helices.
source: The membrane domain of NPC1 contains a sequence of five transmembrane helices that is shared with other membrane proteins whose actions are related to cholesterol (Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes a structural feature of NPC1, supported by citation.

claim: The SSD is shared with other membrane proteins whose actions are related to cholesterol.
source: The membrane domain of NPC1 contains a sequence of five transmembrane helices that is shared with other membrane proteins whose actions are related to cholesterol (Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the evolutionary conservation of the SSD domain.

claim: The SSD contains an intramembrane cleft that has been proposed to bind cholesterol.
source: This sequence, termed the sterol-sensing domain (SSD), contains an intramembrane cleft that has been proposed to bind cholesterol and may function in the transport reaction (Li et al., 2016b).
evidence: This describes a proposed functional feature of the SSD, supported by citation.

claim: The SSD may function in the cholesterol transport reaction.
source: This sequence, termed the sterol-sensing domain (SSD), contains an intramembrane cleft that has been proposed to bind cholesterol and may function in the transport reaction (Li et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the SSD's role, supported by citation.

claim: The structure of full-length NPC1 was determined by cryo-electron microscopy to 4.4 Å resolution.
source: Figure 1B shows the structure of NPC1 as determined by cryo-electron microscopy to 4.4 Å resolution (Gong et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes a structural determination method and resolution, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The NTD is connected to the membrane by a long stalk that extends far enough to cross the ~80 Å glycocalyx.
source: The NTD is connected to the membrane by a long stalk that extends far enough to cross the ~80 Å glycocalyx that shields the lysosomal membrane from lysosomal lipases and proteases.
evidence: This describes the structural feature connecting the NTD to the membrane.

claim: The glycocalyx shields the lysosomal membrane from lysosomal lipases and proteases.
source: The NTD is connected to the membrane by a long stalk that extends far enough to cross the ~80 Å glycocalyx that shields the lysosomal membrane from lysosomal lipases and proteases.
evidence: This describes the protective function of the glycocalyx.

claim: NPC2 transfers cholesterol to the NTD by a sliding mechanism termed the hydrophobic handoff.
source: Cholesterol released from LDL is bound to NPC2 (step 1), which binds to the MLD of NPC1, which orients the NPC2 so that it can transfer its cholesterol to the NTD by a sliding mechanism (step 2) termed the hydrophobic handoff (Kwon et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of cholesterol transfer from NPC2 to NTD, supported by citation.

claim: The transfer of cholesterol from the lumenal NTD to the membranous SSD would require a large conformational change in the protein.
source: The next step is the transfer of cholesterol from the lumenal NTD through the glycocalyx to reach the membranous SSD (step 3). This transfer would require a large conformational change in the protein to re-orient the NTD so that it approaches the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference about the structural changes needed for cholesterol transfer.

claim: X-ray crystallography at 3.3 Å resolution demonstrated that the NTD binds to the CTD.
source: A recent structural analysis of NPC1 by X-ray crystallography at 3.3 Å resolution demonstrated that the NTD binds to the CTD (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a structural finding from X-ray crystallography, supported by citation.

claim: Binding between the NTD and CTD is mediated by the Ω loop that projects from the CTD.
source: Binding is mediated by a short loop designated the Ω loop that projects from the CTD and binds to a region of the NTD.
evidence: This describes the molecular basis of NTD-CTD interaction.

claim: When the Ω loop was deleted from the CTD, the mutant protein traveled normally to lysosomes but failed to transport cholesterol.
source: When the Ω loop was deleted from the CTD, the mutant protein traveled normally to lysosomes, but it failed to transport cholesterol, suggesting that this interaction is crucial for the transfer of cholesterol from the NTD to the membrane (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes experimental results showing the functional importance of the Ω loop.

claim: The interaction between the NTD and the Ω loop is crucial for the transfer of cholesterol from the NTD to the membrane.
source: When the Ω loop was deleted from the CTD, the mutant protein traveled normally to lysosomes, but it failed to transport cholesterol, suggesting that this interaction is crucial for the transfer of cholesterol from the NTD to the membrane (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the deletion mutant experiment.

claim: Full length NPC1, ΔNTD, and NTD-TM1 all localized to lysosomes.
source: Full length NPC1, ΔNTD, and NTD-TM1 all localized to lysosomes as indicated by the yellow color in the merged images.
evidence: This describes experimental results from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: NTD*-TM1 localizes to lysosomes.
source: Two of these proteins localize to lysosomes. One of these, pNTD*-TM1, encodes NTD-TM1 with two amino acid substitutions that eliminate cholesterol binding (P202A/F203A)
evidence: This describes the localization of a mutant construct, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: NPC1(ΔΩ) localizes to lysosomes.
source: Two of these proteins localize to lysosomes. One of these, pNTD*-TM1, encodes NTD-TM1 with two amino acid substitutions that eliminate cholesterol binding (P202A/F203A), and the other, pNPC1(ΔΩ), encodes NPC1 with a deletion of the 9-amino acid loop (designated Ω) that mediates binding to the NTD (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the localization of the Ω loop deletion mutant, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: NTD-TM13 shows a predominant ER localization.
source: The third version of NPC1, NTD-TM13, encodes the NTD followed by the 13th transmembrane helix of NPC1 instead of the first transmembrane helix; it shows a predominant ER localization.
evidence: This describes the localization of a construct with a different transmembrane helix, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: When cholesterol is liberated from lysosomes, it travels to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where it is converted to cholesteryl esters by ACAT.
source: When cholesterol is liberated from lysosomes, it travels to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where it is converted to cholesteryl esters by acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT).
evidence: This describes the metabolic fate of cholesterol after lysosomal export.

claim: When NPC1-/- cells expressing full-length NPC1 were incubated with FCS, LDL-derived cholesterol was transported out of lysosomes and esterified with [14C]oleate.
source: When the cells were incubated with FCS, the LDL-derived cholesterol was transported out of lysosomes and esterified with [14C]oleate (lane 2).
evidence: This describes experimental results from the cholesterol esterification assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No esterification was seen when NPC1-/- cells were transfected with varying amounts of pNTD-TM1.
source: No esterification was seen when we introduced varying amounts of pNTD-TM1, which encodes only the NTD of NPC1 (lanes 3–5).
evidence: This describes experimental results showing that NTD-TM1 alone cannot restore cholesterol transport, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: When NPC1-/- cells expressing ΔNTD were transfected with increasing amounts of NTD-TM1 plasmid, cholesterol transport was restored and cholesteryl [14C]oleate was synthesized.
source: When we transfected increasing amounts of the NTD-TM1 plasmid, cholesterol transport was restored and cholesteryl [14C]oleate was synthesized (lanes 8–10).
evidence: This describes experimental results showing functional complementation, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The NTD can interact functionally with the remainder of NPC1 even when the NTD is not part of the same polypeptide chain.
source: This result indicates that the NTD can interact functionally with the remainder of NPC1 even when the NTD is not part of the same polypeptide chain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the complementation results from Figure 4.

claim: ΔNTD cells exhibit no cholesterol esterification when transfected with a control plasmid, pcDNA3.1.
source: Again, we found that these cells exhibit no cholesterol esterification when transfected with a control plasmid, pcDNA3.1.
evidence: This describes control experimental results, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Esterification was restored when ΔNTD cells were transfected with a plasmid encoding wild type NPC1.
source: Esterification was restored when we transfected a plasmid encoding wild type NPC1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes experimental results showing rescue by wild-type NPC1, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: FCS-dependent esterification was increased when ΔNTD cells expressed NTD-TM1 together with ΔNTD.
source: FCS-dependent esterification was also increased when the cells expressed NTD-TM1 together with ΔNTD (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes experimental results showing functional complementation, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Cholesterol transport was not restored when ΔNTD cells were transfected with NTD-TM13.
source: Esterification was not restored when we expressed NTD-TM13 (Figure 5C), which shows a predominant ER rather than lysosomal localization (see Figure 3).
evidence: This describes experimental results showing lack of complementation by NTD-TM13, with reference to Figures 5C and 3.

claim: Cholesterol transport was not restored when ΔNTD cells were transfected with the P202A/F203A mutant (pNTD*-TM1).
source: Cholesterol transport was also not restored when we transfected the P202A/F203A mutant (pNTD*-TM1), which reaches the lysosome but does not function because it contains two point mutations that prevent cholesterol binding (Figure 5D).
evidence: This describes experimental results showing that cholesterol binding is required for function, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: The P202A/F203A mutant reaches the lysosome but does not function because it contains two point mutations that prevent cholesterol binding.
source: Cholesterol transport was also not restored when we transfected the P202A/F203A mutant (pNTD*-TM1), which reaches the lysosome but does not function because it contains two point mutations that prevent cholesterol binding (Figure 5D).
evidence: This describes the properties of the P202A/F203A mutant, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Deletion of the Ω loop abolished the ability of NPC1 to transport cholesterol out of the lysosome.
source: Deletion of the Ω loop abolished the ability of NPC1 to transport cholesterol out of the lysosome (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a functional consequence of deleting the Ω loop, supported by citation.

claim: When transfected with wild-type NPC1 and incubated with FCS, NPC1-/- cells showed cholesterol esterification.
source: When transfected with wild-type NPC1 and incubated with FCS, the NPC1-/- cells showed the expected cholesterol esterification (lanes 2–4).
evidence: This describes experimental results from Figure 6B showing positive control.

claim: Esterification was not restored when NPC1-/- cells expressed NPC1(ΔΩ).
source: Esterification was not restored when the cells expressed NPC1(ΔΩ) (lanes 5–7).
evidence: This describes experimental results from Figure 6B showing that NPC1(ΔΩ) alone cannot restore function.

claim: In the absence of NPC1(ΔΩ), ΔNTD cells showed no cholesterol esterification.
source: In the absence of NPC1(ΔΩ), these cells showed no cholesterol esterification (Figure 6B, lane 8).
evidence: This describes experimental results from Figure 6B showing baseline lack of function.

claim: FCS-dependent esterification was enhanced when ΔNTD cells co-expressed NPC1(ΔΩ).
source: FCS-dependent esterification was enhanced when the cells co-expressed NPC1(ΔΩ) (lanes 12–14).
evidence: This describes experimental results from Figure 6B showing functional complementation between two full-length NPC1 variants.

claim: LDL-derived cholesterol must pass three hurdles to exit the lysosome: transport to the surface of the glycocalyx, transport across the 80 Å glycocalyx, and transport across the lipid bilayer.
source: In order to exit the lysosome, LDL-derived cholesterol must pass three hurdles: (1) the insoluble sterol must be transported to the surface of the glycocalyx; (2) it must be transported across the 80 Å glycocalyx; and (3) it must be transported across the lipid bilayer that constitutes the lysosomal membrane.
evidence: This describes the three major barriers to cholesterol export from lysosomes.

claim: The first hurdle is overcome by NPC2, which binds cholesterol in the lumen and delivers it to the NTD of NPC1 that lies on the surface of the glycocalyx.
source: The first hurdle is overcome by NPC2, which binds cholesterol in the lumen and delivers it to the NTD of NPC1 that lies on the surface of the glycocalyx.
evidence: This describes how the first barrier is overcome.

claim: Cryo-EM studies demonstrated that the NTD is attached to a proline-rich stalk that is long enough to position the cholesterol-binding site just outside of the glycocalyx where it is accessible to NPC2.
source: Studies using cryo-EM demonstrated that the NTD is attached to a proline-rich stalk that is long enough to position the cholesterol-binding site just outside of the glycocalyx where it is accessible to NPC2 (Gong et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes structural findings from cryo-EM studies, supported by citation.

claim: In order for cholesterol to reach the membrane, either the NTD must move by 80 Å to deliver it there or the cholesterol must be released to an intermediate carrier or channel formed by the MLD and CTD.
source: In order for this cholesterol to reach the membrane, either the NTD must move by 80 Å to deliver it there or the cholesterol must be released to an intermediate carrier or channel that is formed by the MLD and CTD.
evidence: This presents two possible mechanisms for cholesterol transfer across the glycocalyx.

claim: No channel is visible in the structures obtained by cryo-EM or X-ray crystallography.
source: No such channel is visible in the structures obtained by cryo-EM (Gong et al., 2016) or X-ray crystallography (Li et al., 2016b, 2017).
evidence: This describes the absence of a structural feature in published structures, supported by citations.

claim: The NTD can transfer its cholesterol to the membrane even when the NTD is not covalently attached to the remainder of NPC1.
source: In the current paper, we demonstrate that the NTD can transfer its cholesterol to the membrane even when the NTD is not covalently attached to the remainder of NPC1.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data presented in the paper.

claim: Any change in the location of the NTD is mediated by its interactions with the MLD and CTD.
source: This finding suggests that any change in the location of the NTD is mediated by its interactions with the MLD and CTD.
evidence: This is an inference from the complementation experiments.

claim: The NTD of one full-length NPC1 can transfer its cholesterol to another NPC1 that lacks its own NTD.
source: We also show that the NTD of one full-length NPC1 can transfer its cholesterol to another NPC1 that lacks its own NTD.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments with NPC1(ΔΩ) and ΔNTD.

claim: Full-length NPC1 molecules interact with each other.
source: This finding suggests that full-length NPC1 molecules interact with each other, raising the possibility that NPC1 molecules form a complex with each other and that cholesterol transfer results from interactions between neighboring molecules.
evidence: This is an inference from the trans-complementation experiments.

claim: NPC1 molecules may form a complex with each other and cholesterol transfer may result from interactions between neighboring molecules.
source: This finding suggests that full-length NPC1 molecules interact with each other, raising the possibility that NPC1 molecules form a complex with each other and that cholesterol transfer results from interactions between neighboring molecules.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: NPC1 is related by amino acid sequence and structural conformation to a family of bacterial proteins called resistance-nodulation-cell division (RND) proteins.
source: NPC1 is related by amino acid sequence and structural conformation to a family of bacterial proteins called resistance-nodulation-cell division (RND) proteins (Tseng et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the evolutionary relationship between NPC1 and RND proteins, supported by citation.

claim: RND proteins function as proton-coupled antiporters, expelling a variety of structurally unrelated hydrophobic toxins from gram negative bacteria.
source: These proteins function as proton-coupled antiporters, expelling a variety of structurally unrelated hydrophobic toxins from gram negative bacteria (Seeger et al., 2006; Yamaguchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the function of RND proteins, supported by citations.

claim: Like NPC1, RND proteins must transport their cargo across a lipid membrane and across an aqueous space (the periplasm).
source: Like NPC1, RND proteins must transport their cargo across a lipid membrane and across an aqueous space (the periplasm).
evidence: This draws a parallel between the transport challenges faced by NPC1 and RND proteins.

claim: When purified in detergents, RND proteins crystallize as homotrimers.
source: When purified in detergents, RND proteins crystallize as homotrimers.
evidence: This describes the oligomeric state of RND proteins in vitro.

claim: In RND proteins, one of the monomers binds the ligand and undergoes a series of conformational changes that shifts the ligand through a protein-enclosed tunnel until it is discharged on the other side.
source: One of the monomers binds the ligand and undergoes a series of conformational changes that shifts the ligand through a protein-enclosed tunnel until it is discharged on the other side.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of substrate transport by RND proteins.

claim: NPC1 is a monomer when purified in detergents and subjected to cryo-EM or X-ray crystallography.
source: In contrast to RND proteins, NPC1 is a monomer when purified in detergents and subjected to cryo-EM or X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This describes the oligomeric state of NPC1 in structural studies.

claim: The current evidence of interaction between neighboring NPC1 molecules raises the possibility that the protein may form functional multimers in the membrane.
source: Nevertheless, the current evidence of interaction between neighboring NPC1 molecules raises the possibility that the protein may form functional multimers in the membrane and that cholesterol may be transported through the glycocalyx by means of a functional interaction between neighboring NPC1 molecules.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cholesterol may be transported through the glycocalyx by means of a functional interaction between neighboring NPC1 molecules.
source: Nevertheless, the current evidence of interaction between neighboring NPC1 molecules raises the possibility that the protein may form functional multimers in the membrane and that cholesterol may be transported through the glycocalyx by means of a functional interaction between neighboring NPC1 molecules.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of cholesterol transport.

claim: NPC1-/- cells are a stable line of mutant CHO-K1 cells that lack detectable NPC1.
source: NPC1-/- cells (previously referred to as 10–3 cells) are a stable line of mutant CHO-K1 cells that lack detectable NPC1 (Wojtanik and Liscum, 2003).
evidence: This describes the cell line used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: ∆NTD cells are a stable cell line of mutant NPC1-/- cells that stably express human NPC1 lacking the N-terminal domain.
source: ∆NTD cells are a stable cell line of mutant NPC1-/- cells that stably express human NPC1 lacking the N-terminal domain (described below).
evidence: This describes a cell line generated for this study.

claim: The predicted topology of human NPC1 is based on the data of Davies and Ioannou (2000).
source: Predicted topology of human NPC1 based on the data of Davies and Ioannou (2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend, supported by citation.

claim: The structure of full-length NPC1 was accessed from the Protein Data Bank (PDB: 3JD8).
source: Structure of full-length NPC1 as determined by cryo-electron microscopy (Gong et al., 2016) was accessed from the Protein Data Bank (PDB: 3JD8)
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend, indicating the source of the structural data.
